items.title: 71231_Sam Wooding Oral History Interview
items.q: That's when I substituted for Madison Reed for Eubie Blake... So I went on and I followed this thing through. But after that, I played his songs the way he wanted me to.

ctx.x: Do you remember any of the singers there, who they were?

Yes, there was a woman called Mabel Richardson. She was from Washington or Baltimore. She was very good. And there was another one named Alice Jackson, I think, yeah, Alice Jackson. And there was nobody, of course, the ones that you would know more than her, but she was working more with Madison Reed, but that was Mary Stafford, she was with him. Mabel Richardson was almost as good as Mary Stafford, though. And there was another woman called Teddy Peters from out in Chicago, I mean, out along the coast. I asked…

items.title: 71231_Sam Wooding Oral History Interview
items.q: Madison told me, he said, 'I sing that in E-natural.'

ctx.x: No. So, what I substituted for him, and I tell you, to give you an episode, an incident of that which taught me another thing about music.

He asked me to play a song for him, 'All That Worries Me is Someone Else Will Be There When I'm Gone'. You see, a song, on account of the war, people sang, they used this song because it was the draft dodgers, you know, and that was the reason why the guy wrote this song. Well, Madison told me, he said, 'I sing that in E-natural.' Well, as I told you, the colored keys were still a nuisance to me. So, E-natural, I had never bothered, I'd rather not play it. Rather play, put in in E-Flat or F, see what I mean? So I…
